lesson.title: Reisen III: der Ausflug, der Tourist, das Gepäck, der Pass, die Fähre
lesson.subtitle: the day-trip kit — an out-flight, a passport named for walking, and the fahren family's boat

hook.title: The Excursion Set
hook.content: der Ausflug is aus + Flug — an out-flight, fliegen's noun sent outside; English asked Latin instead (excursion is excurrere, 'to run out'), German said it with a verb it owns. das Gepäck is a ge- collective on Pack — and English pack is that same Low German cargo word; one prefix gathers every bag you brought into a single, plural-less noun. der Pass goes back to Latin passus, 'a step' — the same word that gives English pass (to take steps) and pace (a measured step); a border document named for walking through. die Fähre is the fahren family's boat: English faran left fare and ferry behind, German kept fahren and floated the craft itself as die Fähre. And der Tourist is French touriste, from tour, from Latin tornare, 'to turn on a lathe' — a tourist is someone who goes in circles; English tour and turn are the same Latin doublet.

footnotes.title: The ge- That Collects
footnotes.content: German uses ge- to gather many things into one noun: das Gepäck (all the luggage, from Pack), das Gebirge (a whole mountain range, from Berg), das Gemüse (vegetables as one drawer of the fridge). English once owned the same prefix — it survives, fossilized, as the y- of the archaic yclept, 'also called'.

pattern.title: The Day Trip in Frames
pattern.content: Four frames. 1. Go: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge (we take a trip to the mountains) — machen + einen carries the trip. 2. Carry: Das Gepäck ist schwer — singular verb, because das Gepäck is one collective; there is no everyday plural. 3. Documents: Mein Pass ist im Koffer — the one thing you check twice. 4. Cross: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss — and when someone loses the map, Der Tourist sucht den Weg.
pattern.linguist_note: das Gepäck has no everyday plural because the collective prefix already did the plural's job: one word, all the bags. English made the same discovery twice over — luggage (from lug, 'to drag') and baggage are also singular collectives — but it never built a systematic prefix-family the way German did with ge-.

exercises.prompt: The day-trip kit — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: We take a trip to the mountains
matching_pairs.german: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge

matching_pairs.english: My passport is in the suitcase
The ferry goes across the river
matching_pairs.german: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss

matching_pairs.english: The tourist looks for the stop
The excursion by bike goes across the mountains
matching_pairs.german: Der Ausflug mit dem Fahrrad geht quer durch die Berge

matching_pairs.english: Tomatoes and fruit for the excursion
matching_pairs.german: Tomaten und Obst für den Ausflug

matching_pairs.english: The way into the village is far
matching_pairs.german: Der Weg ins Dorf ist weit

matching_pairs.english: The tourist has a hat and a bag
matching_pairs.german: Der Tourist hat einen Hut und eine Tasche

matching_pairs.english: In August or in September we take the excursion
matching_pairs.german: Im August oder im September machen wir den Ausflug
Die Abfahrt und die Ankunft der Fähre

exercises.target_answer: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge, Das Gepäck ist schwer, Mein Pass ist im Koffer, Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss, Der Tourist sucht die Haltestelle, Die Fahrkarte für die Fähre, Der Ausflug mit dem Fahrrad geht quer durch die Berge, Tomaten und Obst für den Ausflug, Der Weg ins Dorf ist weit, Der Tourist hat einen Hut und eine Tasche, Im August oder im September machen wir den Ausflug, Die Abfahrt und die Ankunft der Fähre
exercises.meaning: excursion, luggage, passport, ferry, tourist, harbor
exercises.explanation: Six day-trip frames from five new nouns and the verbs you own: machen carries the Ausflug, fährt drives die Fähre, sucht is suchen looking for den Weg. Das Gepäck stays singular even when it is heavy.

exercises.prompt: 'Der Ausflug' is an out-trip — aus + the noun of a verb you own. Which verb is hiding inside it?
exercises.explanation: der Flug is fliegen's noun, and aus sends it outside: an out-flight. English asked Latin for the same idea — excursion is excurrere, 'to run out' — while German compounded the verb it already had.

exercises.prompt: die Fähre is the boat of the fahren family. English kept the same root as the verb for what a trip costs (fare) and as the craft that carries you. Which is die Fähre's twin?
exercises.meaning: die Fähre ↔ ferry: the fahren family's boat
exercises.explanation: ferry is Old English ferian, 'to carry', the causative twin of faran — the verb German keeps as fahren. fairy (Latin fata), furrow (a ploughing word) and farrow (a litter of pigs) are look-alikes from different families.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the crossing sentence: 'The ferry goes across the river'
exercises.target_answer: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss
exercises.meaning: The ferry goes across the river
exercises.explanation: fährt is the same fahren you drive a Zug with — here it is the boat doing the driving. über + den (accusative) marks the crossing, and the bank's Meer and Wasser are the bigger crossings waiting: über das Meer.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I have my passport and the luggage'
exercises.target_answer: Ich habe meinen Pass und das Gepäck
exercises.meaning: I have my passport and the luggage
exercises.explanation: meinen Pass — der Pass takes the masculine -en after mein. und joins a masculine document and a neuter collective without changing stride: der Pass, das Gepäck, one sentence.

summary.outcome: Pack the day trip: Ausflug, Gepäck, Pass, Fähre, Tourist — and know which verb or Latin step each one carries.

use_example.german: Wir machen einen Ausflug — die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
use_example.english: We take an excursion — the ferry goes across the river.

summary.takeaway: Ausflug = aus + Flug (excursion is Latin 'run out'); Gepäck is the ge-collective of English pack; Pass is Latin passus 'step'; Fähre is ferry of the fahren family; Tourist is a turner of circles.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: five countries — Deutschland, Frankreich, England, Spanien, Italien — and why English renamed two of them.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Reisen III: der Ausflug, der Tourist, das Gepäck, der Pass, die Fähre (I have my passport and the luggage):
twist.target_answer: Ich habe meinen Pass und das Gepäck
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich habe meinen Pass und das Gepäck" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Reisen III: der Ausflug, der Tourist, das Gepäck, der Pass, die Fähre without relying on short-term echo.

ausflug.context_phrase: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge.
ausflug.context_translation: We take a trip to the mountains.
ausflug.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly): literally an out-flight, an excursion. [wiktionary]

tourist.context_phrase: Der Tourist fragt nach dem Weg.
tourist.context_translation: The tourist asks for the way.
tourist.etymology_derivation: Tour (tour, turn) + -ist; the page says it was formed in the 18th century, possibly influenced by English tourist being made at the same time from the same French material. [wiktionary]

gepäck.context_phrase: Mein Gepäck ist noch nicht da.
gepäck.context_translation: My luggage is not here yet.
gepäck.etymology_derivation: A collective of Pack (bundle) — the Low German packing word English also took as pack. [wiktionary]

pass.etymology_derivation: From Old French pas, from Latin passus (step); the passport sense is a shortening of French passeport, the same source English used. [wiktionary]

fähre.context_phrase: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
fähre.context_translation: The ferry goes across the river.
fähre.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *farjo, the ferrying word of the same far-root as fahren — the page lists English ferry as cognate. [wiktionary]

fahrkarte.context_phrase: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Berlin.
fahrkarte.context_translation: I buy a ticket to Berlin.
fahrkarte.etymology_derivation: fahren (to travel, the fare root) + Karte (card, from Latin charta — the same loan as English card): a travel-card. [wiktionary]

fahrplan.context_phrase: Der Fahrplan hängt an der Wand.
fahrplan.context_translation: The timetable hangs on the wall.
fahrplan.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Plan (plan, the same French-Latin word English uses): the travel-plan, a timetable. [wiktionary]

fahrrad.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Rad (wheel): the driving-wheel. [wiktionary]

quer.context_phrase: Der Baum liegt quer über dem Weg.
quer.context_translation: The tree lies across the path.
quer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *þwerh, oblique (Old High German twerh); etymonline lists German quer as a cognate of English thwart, from Old Norse þverr, across. [wiktionary][etymonline]

fisch.context_translation: The fish swims in the water.

obst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *obaet; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

tomate.context_phrase: Die Tomate ist rot und reif.
tomate.context_translation: The tomato is red and ripe.
tomate.etymology_derivation: From Spanish/French tomate, Classical Nahuatl tomatl — the same New World loan as English tomato. [wiktionary]

gurke.context_phrase: Die Gurke ist frisch und grün.
gurke.context_translation: The cucumber is fresh and green.
gurke.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, Greek angoúrion — cognate with English gherkin. [wiktionary]

kartoffel.etymology_derivation: From Tartuffel, from Italian tartufolo 'truffle', Latin terrae tūber 'earth tuber'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

zwiebel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed early from Late Latin cēpulla; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

weit.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīdaz — the direct cognate of English wide. [wiktionary]

blau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *blēwaz; English blue (via French bleu) is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

grau.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *grāu — English gray is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

hut.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hōdaz — Wiktionary's English cognate is hood, not hat. See Fingerhut. [wiktionary]

tasche.etymology_derivation: Perhaps Proto-Germanic *taskǭ; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

koffer.etymology_derivation: Through Middle Dutch from Old French cofre — the French loan English also took as coffer and coffin. [wiktionary]

dorf.context_phrase: Das Dorf liegt hinter dem Berg.
dorf.context_translation: The village lies behind the mountain.
dorf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *thurpa — Old English thorp, which survives in English place names like Mablethorpe; the English th hardened into German d. [wiktionary]

markt.context_phrase: Auf dem Markt kaufe ich Obst.
markt.context_translation: At the market I buy fruit.
markt.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *markat, an early Latin borrowing shared with English market. [wiktionary]

haltestelle.context_translation: The bus stop is right here.
haltestelle.etymology_derivation: halten (to hold) + Stelle (place, from the same old place-root as English stall): a hold-place, where the vehicle stops. [wiktionary]

abfahrt.context_phrase: Die Abfahrt ist um neun Uhr.
abfahrt.context_translation: The departure is at nine o'clock.
abfahrt.etymology_derivation: The noun of abfahren: ab (off) + Fahrt (the fare root) — literally an off-driving, a departure. [wiktionary]

ankunft.context_phrase: Die Ankunft ist um halb sieben.
ankunft.context_translation: The arrival is at half past six.
ankunft.etymology_derivation: From ankommen (to arrive) — an on-coming; kommen is the German twin of come. [wiktionary]

august.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Augustus. [wiktionary]

september.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin September, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

schiff.etymology_derivation: P → FF shift. Cognate with English "ship" and living nautical twin "skipper" (literally Schiff-er, ship-master).

meer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. English mere is the listed cognate, and Latin mare is cognate through Indo-European. [wiktionary]

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

schwer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swēraz 'heavy, grave'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
